linkedin_post.angle: The first Bold batch failed in my kitchen at 6 AM. That failure is why the jar on your shelf works.
linkedin_post.hook: I watched our pilot Bold batch die in the cup before the timer hit 12 seconds. That hollow cup forced us to walk away from a signed contract and start over.
linkedin_post.body:
We had the pilot lot of Purity Beans Bold on the cupping table. Agglomerated pure coffee, zero chicory. The roast was right. The grind was right. But the first brew collapsed — crema vanished, aroma evaporated, cup hollow before it cooled. The panel tasted it. I tasted it. The moment was gone.

We could have launched it. The contract was signed. The margins were real. But the label would have promised pure coffee while the cup delivered disappointment.

We walked away. Switched to a slower agglomeration run that traps the oils inside the granules. Higher cost. Lower throughput. But the crema holds. The aroma lingers. The kick stays clean to the last sip.

The morning after the switch, I brewed the new Purity Beans Bold at 6 AM in my kitchen. No panel. No spoon. Just a mug, hot water, and a single expectation. The aroma did not fade. It deepened — roasted, honest, persistent. The crema held. The kick lasted.

That mug told me what data could not: the label is the only contract that matters. If the cup does not keep the promise on the jar, the label lied.

## What does freeze-dried instant coffee mean for an Indian kitchen?

Freeze-dried instant coffee means the brewed liquid was frozen solid and the ice lifted away under vacuum, leaving behind light, porous granules that dissolve the moment they hit hot water. In an Indian kitchen, that translates to a cup that keeps the coffee’s original aroma instead of the flat, burnt note you get from high-heat spray drying. You’ll notice the difference most when you drink it black — no milk, no sugar — because the caramel and chocolate tones in a good Arabica or the deep, nutty body of a Robusta actually come through. A practical tip: warm your mug with a splash of hot water first, then add the granules; the temperature shock is gentler and the flavor opens up faster. Purity Beans uses this method for Purica and Purista, both 100g jars priced at ₹559 and ₹509 respectively, while Ultra Blend stays at 70% coffee and 30% chicory for a milder everyday cup. Prima is pure Arabica but agglomerated, so it behaves differently in the cup.

### A plain definition

Whatever brought you here, the label settles it. The other single jars on this page are 0% chicory.

## How do you read the chicory line on the jar?

Flip the jar over. The ingredient list is the only line that matters, and it is always in descending order by weight. If chicory appears first, that jar is mostly chicory. If chicory is absent entirely, you have pure coffee. I keep a Purity Beans jar on my shelf because the label reads simply: coffee. No fillers, no footnotes. A concrete habit: next time you are in the aisle, pick up three jars and compare the first two ingredients side by side. The difference is instant and undeniable. Price is a clue, too — a 100g jar of pure freeze-dried Arabica at ₹559 or Robusta at ₹509 reflects the bean cost, while a 100g blend at ₹309 reflects the filler. Your palate will thank you for checking.

## Which jar suits the way you drink coffee?

Choosing a jar comes down to what your morning actually looks like. If you take your coffee black and want that deep, full-bodied kick, Bold (₹239 for 50g) is the workhorse — agglomerated granules that dissolve fast and deliver a strong, honest cup. When the mood shifts to something smoother, Purica (₹329 for 50g) brings pure Arabica with natural caramel and chocolatey notes, while Purista (₹319 for 50g) gives you gourmet Robusta with a rich crema and bold-yet-smooth character; both are freeze-dried, so the aroma stays locked in until you open the jar. Can't decide? The Variety Box (₹877) puts all four 50g jars on your counter for a proper tasting flight, and the Gourmet Duo Mini (₹570) pairs just the two freeze-dried jars side by side. Pro tip: brew a small cup of each black first — no sugar, no milk — and you'll taste the difference instantly. Purity Beans keeps the lineup simple so you can match the jar to the ritual.

## What does each jar cost in rupees?

A 50g jar of Purica Gourmet Arabica Granules is ₹329, and the 100g jar is ₹559. Purista Gourmet Robusta Granules come in at ₹319 for 50g and ₹509 for 100g. Both are freeze-dried and contain zero chicory. Bold Pure Coffee uses an agglomerated process instead; the 50g jar is ₹239 and the 100g jar is ₹369, also with no chicory added. If you want to taste the two freeze-dried jars side by side, the Gourmet Duo Mini gives you 50g of Purista and 50g of Purica for ₹570, while the full-size Gourmet Duo pairs 100g of each for ₹908. ## How do people brew instant coffee in Indian cities?

In Indian city kitchens, the mug-and-kettle method still rules most mornings. Water hits a rolling boil, someone spoons coffee into a favorite cup, and the pour begins — slow enough to let the aroma climb before the first sip. A pinch of sugar, a splash of milk, and the day officially starts. Offices that keep a French press on the pantry shelf get a richer body with almost no extra effort, while cold-brew jars tucked in the fridge overnight save ten frantic minutes before a Zoom call. One friend swears by blooming the granules with a teaspoon of room-temperature water for thirty seconds before the hot pour; she says it wakes up the volatiles that boiling water alone can flatten. On weekends the same routine stretches: a steel filter, a slow drip, and a quiet half-hour with the newspaper.

Stand in the aisle and turn the jar around. The front will always promise rich aroma and bold flavor, but the back tells the real story. Look for the ingredient list first: if it says coffee and chicory, you are buying a blend, not pure coffee. Next, check the process. Neither is better; they just suit different rituals. Price per gram matters too. A 100g jar of Purica at ₹559 works out cheaper per cup than the 50g at ₹329 if you drink it daily. Finally, trust your palate over marketing words. Buy a small jar, brew it black, and taste. If it finishes clean without that powdery aftertaste, you have found your jar. editorial_score.feedback: This poll post fails on every growth metric. The headline 'STRONG BLACK COFFEE: BOLD OR PURICA?' is a category label, not a hook — it creates zero curiosity, zero tension, and zero identity trigger. A scroll-stopping hook must land in under 2 seconds with betrayal, curiosity gap, identity challenge, or contrarian statement. This does none of those. The subtext 'Same pure coffee, different process' is passive education, not a reason to engage. The poll question 'Which process for your black cup?' assumes the audience already cares about agglomerated vs freeze-dried — they don't, not without a 'why this matters to YOU' frame. Option B's copy 'Bold is agglomerated pure coffee' reads like a spec sheet, not a consumer benefit. No emotional trigger (pride, betrayal, relief, curiosity) is activated. The comment trigger 'Comment the first word you see on the jar label' is a generic engagement hack unrelated to the poll topic — it feels like a bot prompt. Save/share triggers are generic templates ('real coffee matters', 'starts every morning with coffee') that could apply to any brand. Brand clarity is the only passing dimension because the product names appear, but without a clear POV on WHY Bold vs Purica matters to the drinker, Purity Beans is not positioned as the obvious authority. To fix: rewrite the hook as a betrayal or identity challenge ('Most people pick the wrong process for black coffee — here's why'), frame the poll as a revelation ('Your black coffee deserves freeze-dried. growth_reel_fb.caption:
How many times have you heard that cafés pour unsold brewed coffee into a “special” batch and serve it to the next customer? At home, we simply toss the jar when the grind runs out. The truth is far more interesting. 

A café’s leftover brew is a mixture of water, coffee oils, and fine coffee particles that have already been extracted – the flavor profile is already set, and the beans have given up most of their soluble compounds. In contrast, an agglomerated jar like Bold contains pure coffee granules that re‑hydrate instantly, preserving the original bean characteristics each time you stir. 

Bold is made from pure Arabica beans sourced from high‑altitude farms where each cherry is hand‑picked at peak ripeness. The beans are roasted to a medium‑dark level that brings out chocolatey notes without the burnt edge you get from over‑extracted café brew. 

So the next time you see a “coffee‑reuse” sign at a coffee shop, ask yourself: are you getting the same fresh‑taste experience you can achieve in seconds with a jar of pure agglomerated coffee? 

Let’s talk – what’s your go‑to method for handling leftover coffee at home?
